To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the rates of N15 incorporation into chromosomal proteins and into cytoplasmic proteins are parallel in all tissues studied.
the histones and the residual proteins of the chromosome are not synthesized de novo in the cell, but are synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transferred to the chromosome.

the rates of N15 incorporation into the histone and the residual protein fractions of the chromatin are lower than those of the cytoplamic proteins, and that the rate of N15 loss from the chromosomal proteins is greater when the animal is fed than when it is fasted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of protein turnover in the cell.
a comparative analysis of the metabolism of the protein fractions of the cell, particularly those of the nucleus and cytoplasm.
the problem of the relationship between the metabolism of cytoplasmic proteins and the histones and other proteins of chromosomes of non-dividing cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chromosomal protein is synthesized in the cytoplasm and is transported to the chromosome.

, while the histones and other proteins of the chromosomes do not participate in protein synthesis in non-dividing cells to the extent that the proteins of the ribonucleoproteins of the cytoplam do, they do participate, though to a much lesser extent.

the chromosomal protein fractions, like the cytoplasmic ones, are responsive to environmental changes and that the rates of glycinc-N15 uptake by them parallel the rates of incorporation by the cytoplasm as a whole.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the histones and the residual proteins of chromatin are metabolized at rates which are comparable to those for the cytoplasmic proteins.
the histones and the residual chromosomal proteins are synthesized at a low rate and that the rate of synthesis is responsive to changes in the general level of protein metabolism.
the histones and the residual protein fraction of the chromosomes are not metabolically inert but are responsive to environmental changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chromosomal proteins are not inert, and they are not static.
the rates of protein synthesis are not different between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, but that the rates of loss from chromosomal proteins are different.
the histone proteins are the most stable of the chromosomal proteins, and that their synthesis is not a major source of nitrogen for chromosomal protein synthesis.
